2026-10-10 / Project Confluence / Development note

Project Confluence — From Technical Experiments to District Blockout

The first development phase of Project Confluence connects climate-adaptive urban design with practical UE5 experiments in parameter-driven construction, environmental materials, rendering, and district blockout.

Establish an environment direction

Project Confluence is an ongoing Environment Technical Art study exploring climate-adaptive high-density urbanism. Its central idea is that a future city continuously adapts its inherited infrastructure instead of replacing it.

The worldbuilding direction combines mountainous island settlements, dense mixed-use development, ecological infrastructure, and rail-based public transportation. Local trams follow the islands' urban corridors, while cross-sea railways belong to a separate regional network.

The current production focus is one representative coastal district, not the entire city. Establishing a coherent relationship between everyday urban life, steep terrain, public transit, and the ocean is the first environment design challenge.

The District Master Plan v0.1 explores how the station, neighborhood streets, residential areas, public spaces, and vertical circulation might connect across three terrain levels. These are planning proposals that still require validation in Unreal Engine.

Explore parameter-driven construction

Before beginning the formal environment, I used a separate UE5 sandbox to learn Blueprint workflows through small experiments.

One procedural Actor uses exposed module count, mesh, and spacing parameters to construct repeated Static Mesh Components in the editor. The Construction Script allows changes to regenerate the arrangement without manually replacing each component.

The two examples demonstrate the same Blueprint with different module counts and spacing values. This establishes a basic parameter-driven construction workflow without committing to a full procedural city system.

Prototype environmental wetness

The next experiment focused on material behavior. After exploring Material Instances, Material Functions, UVs, and world-aligned mapping, I developed an initial MF_WaterlineWetness prototype.

The function calculates a height-based wetness mask using world-space position relative to an adjustable waterline. Additional noise controls introduce variation along the boundary and transition region.

The tests separate the visible material response from the underlying mask, making it easier to inspect where the transition occurs.

Investigate real-time rendering

Further experiments explored exposure, atmospheric fog, Lumen global illumination, reflections, and Nanite visualization.

A simple red-surface lighting study was used to inspect how material color and indirect illumination influence surrounding surfaces. The experiments helped establish an initial understanding of Unreal Engine's rendering workflow before environmental art production.

Begin the coastal district blockout

With the initial engine studies completed, I created the formal ProjectConfluence project and its first working level, L_District_Blockout_01.

The current Landscape covers approximately 252 × 504 meters, with three principal terrain elevations around 30m, 50m, and 70m. Initial graybox work establishes building masses, a local coastal tram corridor and station, bridge approaches, steep terrain, and distant-island context.

The first blockout prioritizes terrain hierarchy, transit alignment, building placement, and the overall relationship between the inhabited terraces and the ocean.

The current planning iteration examines how the station area, middle neighborhood street, upper residential zone, and connecting pedestrian routes might form a coherent district. These circulation proposals have not yet been fully implemented.

Scope and next steps

Confluence remains in early development.

The current district is a graybox environment, while the Blueprint, material, and rendering experiments were developed separately in the UE5 learning sandbox.

Procedural city generation, dynamic water behavior, final environmental assets, and the full transit system have not yet been implemented.

The next phase focuses on validating pedestrian circulation, architectural massing, terrain connections, and transit geometry before developing more advanced procedural environment tools.

The objective is to build a coherent, technically grounded environment rather than expand the city before its fundamental spatial relationships are resolved.
